chief_complaint: severe fatigue, pale skin, cold hands, and heavy menstrual bleeding
hpi_details: 24F reports 6 months of worsening fatigue, feeling out of breath when climbing stairs, cold hands/feet, and pale skin. Mentions her menstrual periods are very heavy, lasting 7-8 days and requiring double pads.
ideas: thinks she is just overworked and needs iron supplements
concerns: worried about leukemia or blood cancer

clinical_knowledge.topic: Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia (secondary to menorrhagia) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia (secondary to menorrhagia) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for severe iron deficiency anemia secondary to menorrhagia, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Heavy, prolonged menstrual periods (menorrhagia) requiring double pads
Progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness over 6 months
Pallor and cold extremities suggesting significant anemia
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia (secondary to menorrhagia).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Anemia of chronic disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Chest pain or severe breathlessness — may need urgent transfusion if anemia is severe.
management_principles: Order CBC (microcytic anemia), ferritin, iron panel
Start oral Ferrous Sulfate 325mg daily with Vitamin C
Refer to gynecology for evaluation and management of menorrhagia
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 24F with 6 months of worsening fatigue, exertional breathlessness, cold hands/feet, and pale skin, in the setting of heavy menstrual periods lasting 7-8 days and requiring double pads.
reference_soap.objective: Pale conjunctiva and pale skin. Mild tachycardia. Cool extremities. No koilonychia noted.
reference_soap.assessment: Severe iron deficiency anemia secondary to menorrhagia.
reference_soap.plan: Order CBC (microcytic anemia), ferritin, iron panel. Start oral Ferrous Sulfate 325mg daily with Vitamin C. Refer to gynecology for evaluation of menorrhagia and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia secondary to menorrhagia.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for severe fatigue, pale skin, cold hands, and heavy menstrual bleeding
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for hematology & oncology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia secondary to menorrhagia.

teaching.diagnosis: Severe Iron Deficiency Anemia (secondary to menorrhagia)
teaching.one_liner: Chronic blood loss from heavy periods depletes iron stores faster than they can be replaced, causing fatigue, pallor, and cold extremities from reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.
differentials: GI blood loss (if menstrual history doesn't fully explain it)
red_flags: Chest pain or severe breathlessness — may need urgent transfusion if anemia is severe

must_ask.say: How many days do your periods last, and how often do you need to change pads?
How long have you been feeling this tired?
Do you get short of breath going up stairs?
Have your hands and feet felt unusually cold, or has your skin looked pale?
How much iron-rich food, like red meat, do you typically eat?

history.answer: I have been feeling completely exhausted all the time for the past few months, and people at work keep pointing out how pale I look.
It feels like a total lack of energy and I get winded so easily, rather than just feeling sleepy during the day.
It started about 6 months ago and has gotten progressively worse, without any specific illness or event triggering it.
It is really hard to concentrate and finish tasks at my desk job, and resting over the weekend does not help at all.
I wake up tired and stay exhausted all day, but it feels even more draining toward the late afternoon.
I sleep about 7 to 8 hours every night without waking up, and I do not snore or choke in my sleep.
My mood is fine and I still enjoy spending time on my hobbies, with no depressive feelings or thoughts of self-harm.
I feel lightheaded when I stand up quickly, but my bowel movements are normal brown with no red blood or black tarry stools.
My periods last 7 to 8 days and are very heavy with large clots, so I have to wear two pads at once.
No, I have not noticed any easy bruising on my arms or legs, and my gums do not bleed when brushing.
No, I do not have any numbness, tingling, or pins and needles in my fingers or toes.
Yes, my hands and feet always feel freezing cold, and my skin has looked very washed out and pale.
Aside from my cold hands and feet, I have not had unusual cold intolerance, unexpected weight gain, constipation, or dry skin.
No, I do not have extreme thirst and I do not need to urinate more frequently than usual.
My skin has not gotten darker at all, and my appetite has remained fairly normal.
No, I have no itchy skin, no changes in how food tastes, and my urine output is normal.
No fever, chills, or night sweats, and my weight has remained completely stable.
I get noticeably short of breath just walking up one flight of stairs, but my legs have not been swelling.
I eat three meals a day, but I rarely eat red meat and usually stick to simple salads and grain bowls.
I thought maybe I was just burnt out from work stress and needed some over-the-counter iron pills.
A coworker mentioned that looking this pale and drained could be leukemia, which really terrified me.
I would like to have my blood counts checked to find out what is causing this severe fatigue.
Work gets busy around month-end, but my stress is manageable; I drink one cup of coffee a day and no energy drinks.
I have never had any chronic medical conditions or long-term health problems.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, pain relievers, or daily supplements right now.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes.
I only drink a glass of beer once or twice a month on social occasions.
I work as an office clerk and live independently in an apartment.
No one in my family has a history of anemia, bleeding disorders, or blood cancers.
My last period started two weeks ago; I have regular 28-day cycles, am not sexually active, and cannot be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 105/68 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C.
Marked bilateral palpebral conjunctival pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
Diffuse pallor and cool extremities bilaterally; no koilonychia, petechiae, or purpura.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and without palpable nodules.
Mildly tachycardic regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without wheezing or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with normal bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly.
No pretibial pitting edema on either lower extremity.
